name: Original Plum Torte
headnote: Marian Burros's plum torte ran in The Times every September from 1983 through 1989, when editors tried to retire it and were buried in protest mail from readers who treated its annual appearance as the official end of summer. The paper gave in and now keeps it permanently available. The recipe carries two sugar amounts: the original 1983 cup and the reduced three-quarters cup from 1989, and both are printed.
comment_digest: The single most-voted note (4,606) is a question nobody should have to ask: does '1 cup flour, sifted' mean sift before or after measuring? A high-voted reply (4,106) settles it - 'sifted flour' means sift then measure, 'flour, sifted' means measure then sift, so here you measure first. Bakers report the batter is thin and barely covers the pan bottom; that is correct, it rises around the fruit. Substitutions are near-universal and work: raspberries, blackberries, apricots, Italian prune plums, and one commenter swapped a third of the flour for cornmeal. Several recommend slicing plums and fanning them rather than using halves, for prettier and more even distribution, and adding lemon zest. The torte freezes well, which is the reason many make several at once in plum season.

name: Pan-Seared Tilefish with Garlic, Herbs and Lemon
headnote: A basic sauteed fish fillet that the headnote argues every cook should know. The one step that looks harder than it is: spooning the pan fat back over the fish as it cooks, which cooks it evenly and keeps it moist. The fat here is butter, which browns and turns nutty as the fish cooks. Tilefish is named but any firm fillet - sea bass, grouper - substitutes.
comment_digest: Very few comments, but they agree on the method more than the fish. The top note (45 votes) cooked it with tilefish straight off the Outer Banks and swapped shallots for scallions and dried basil for fresh with no loss. A dissent worth noting (19 votes) warns that tilefish is high in methyl mercury and points to the Monterey Bay Aquarium guide, suggesting another species. Others confirm the basting technique transfers: one used it on halibut cheeks, another on supermarket cod, both successfully. Repeated advice is to use a generous amount of butter, roughly a tablespoon per person, and to get the pan properly hot before the fish goes in. Fresh garden herbs are what several credit for the dish.

name: Pappardelle with Greens and Ricotta
headnote: A fast pasta pitched at dinner-party cooking when there is no time to prep ahead. The headnote's one real instruction is to hunt down fresh ricotta from an Italian market rather than the supermarket tub.
comment_digest: The top note (78 votes) rewrites the workflow: chop the greens raw and throw them into the pasta water for the last minute instead of cooking them separately, then drain both together - one pot, less time. Close behind (76 votes), a cook substituted Bulgarian sheep's-milk feta for the ricotta and reports it worked better, being softer and sharper. That points at the recipe's main complaint: as written it reads bland, and people fix it with anchovies, cherry tomatoes sauteed with the garlic, lemon, or red pepper flakes. Counter to the headnote, several say freshly made ricotta melts into the sauce and disappears, and that a firmer store-bought one holds its texture better. Any pasta shape works; spaghetti and penne both reported fine.

name: Parmesan-Crusted Rack of Lamb
headnote: A rack of lamb adapted from an old Escoffier recipe, coated so the outside turns salty and crunchy against the sweet roasted meat. It is pitched as a dinner-party showpiece served alongside Macaroni Milanaise, with the headnote noting how little work it actually takes.
comment_digest: The two highest-voted notes are both about timing: 20 minutes in the oven is too long for rare or medium-rare, so use a thermometer rather than the clock (32 votes); another got a perfect medium-rare at 400F for about 25 minutes (31 votes), searing and roasting in the same cast-iron skillet to save a pan. The loudest recurring correction is the missing garlic - multiple cooks (30 and 26 votes) add two or more crushed cloves during the sear or into the crumb mix, and call it essential. Rosemary in the dry mix is the other common addition. A well-liked variation brushes the seared rack with Dijon before the cheese and breadcrumbs go on, which helps the crust adhere and adds sharpness.

name: Pasta Alla Genovese
headnote: La Genovese is a Neapolitan beef sauce that many in the city regard as the center of its cooking, despite being almost nothing but a huge quantity of onions and beef simmered until both collapse. The recipe boils the onions first as a time-saving departure from tradition, though the headnote concedes the saving is modest. Slicing them raw and simply cooking longer is the more orthodox route.
comment_digest: The top comment (287 votes), from a cook in Naples, says the recipe is missing white wine - it belongs in with the meat - and that the cut matters: use rump, as for pot roast. Onion handling is the other big thread. A widely endorsed technique (160 votes) layers sliced onions with salt under water and a weighted plate to press them before cooking; several others (82, 97 votes) simply skip the boiling step entirely, calling it a scald that adds little, and sweat the raw sliced onions instead. Time is the real ingredient: one Neapolitan chef reportedly runs his for 16 hours on the lowest possible flame. Expect a rich, glossy, almost creamy sauce. Halving the recipe works for two.

name: Pasta with Bacon, Cheese, Lemon and Pine Nuts
headnote: The pitch is a modular family dinner: start with a plain base of pasta, butter and cheese that picky eaters will accept, then set out pine nuts, lemon zest, brown butter, bacon and herbs so everyone builds their own bowl. The framing comes from a piece on feeding a table with incompatible tastes.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (324) is a set of upgrades: pancetta instead of bacon, half butter and half olive oil, dry-toast the pine nuts in a skillet first, and grate the lemon zest in for brightness. The clearest correction (129 votes) is that four tablespoons of butter is far too much for the amount of cheese - cut it well back; a scaled-for-two version (248 votes) uses about three-quarters of a tablespoon. Because the sauce comes together fast, several warn to have it ready before the pasta drains, or the noodles sit and turn sticky. One cook oven-baked whole bacon strips on a foil-lined sheet to make doubling easy. Bucatini gets a specific endorsement.

name: Perfect Peach Pie
headnote: The argument is that a truly great fresh peach is rare - one or two a season - but a pie reliably lifts merely good fruit, and works even with frozen peaches. Sugar does the heavy lifting, with lemon juice and a little nutmeg added for a touch of bitterness against the sweetness. Vanilla ice cream is suggested for a diner-style finish.
comment_digest: A runny filling is the recurring failure, and the top note (866 votes) fixes it by macerating the sliced peaches in the sugar first and draining off the released juice before filling the shell; a corroborating comment (262) cites Cook's Illustrated doing the same and then thickening with cornstarch slaked in a little of the reserved juice. Peeling is contested: a well-voted note (328) argues skins on give the filling more body and color, and another (287) confirms leaving them on works fine, while others recommend a soft-fruit peeler over blanching. Thickener choice affects appearance - tapioca sets clear, flour cloudy. Bake on a low rack (220 votes) to crisp the bottom crust; blind baking is also endorsed.

name: Pizza with Caramelized Onions, Ricotta and Chard
headnote: A rich vegetable pizza: caramelized onions spread over a base of ricotta, Parmesan and chopped Swiss chard. It came out of a piece on cooking chard in a cold spring. The headnote is brief and offers no technique notes.
comment_digest: Two practical themes dominate a thin comment set. First, it needs acid or heat - cooks add red pepper flakes, a balsamic drizzle, or green olives for salt, and the top note (38 votes) reports arugula in place of the greens working well. Second, the recipe dirties too many pans (14 votes): one cook caramelized the onions, then wilted the chopped chard with garlic in the same skillet and assembled from there. Chard swaps freely with spinach or kale. Baking time runs short of what the recipe implies - one finished in about six minutes - so watch it. A cast-iron pan bottom stands in for a pizza pan and gives a crisper crust.

name: Porchetta Pork Chops
headnote: Melissa Clark's shortcut on porchetta: the garlic, rosemary and fennel seasoning of the whole roast pig, applied to pork chops instead. The pitch is that it comes together fast enough to be a spur-of-the-moment weeknight dinner rather than a project.
comment_digest: Overcooking is the trap. Multiple high-voted notes (158, 101) warn to follow the stated times rather than instinct - cooks who added a minute at each stage ended up with dry chops, and anyone working with thinner chops than Clark's needs to cut the time further. A thermometer is the standard advice. The top note (374 votes) enriches the herb filling with a teaspoon of Dijon and two diced anchovies. A well-liked adaptation (318 votes) scales the same garlic-herb paste to a butterflied pork loin for a bigger meal. Others prefer thyme to half the rosemary, and finish with a white-wine pan sauce. One dissent (105 votes) finds the flavors harsh and calls the 20-minute time estimate unrealistic.

name: Pork Ragù Al Maialino
headnote: Sam Sifton's home adaptation of a restaurant ragu that began as a way to use up leftovers, stripped of the suckling pig, fresh pasta and veal stock the original relied on. Cheap pork shoulder and extra butter stand in, and the result is meant to taste like restaurant cooking anyway.
comment_digest: Make it a day ahead - the top-rated practical note (42 votes) tears the meat while still warm, refrigerates, and says it improves overnight; it also converts pork skeptics. Browning the pork before softening the aromatics is the most common addition (several notes) for deeper flavor, though the recipe does not call for it. Expect roughly 2.5 hours of cooking. Boneless pork butt or cubed shoulder both work, and red wine plus water substitutes acceptably for stock. An Instant Pot version is reported as reliable and easy to scale up or down. Pappardelle is the preferred pasta. The comment set is small, with no real disagreement about the method.

name: Red Beans and Rice
headnote: Kim Severson's version of the Monday-night New Orleans staple, as made by the late food writer Pableaux Johnson, who fed a rotating table of writers and musicians on it. The dish dates from when Monday was laundry day and the beans were built on the leftover pork bone from Sunday. Louisiana andouille is the sausage to look for; smoked sausage is the fallback.
comment_digest: The dominant note (1,801 votes) comes from a native New Orleans family: soak the beans only about 10 minutes, boil 20, then let them sit off the heat until cooking time; mash some of the beans near the end for creaminess and finish with a little butter. That creaminess is the point most commenters insist on. The second-most-voted note (1,120) says the dish is nearly impossible to ruin and treats the recipe as a template. Practical additions with strong support: a couple of splashes of vinegar at the end for acid (325 votes), and an Instant Pot conversion that skips soaking entirely (464 votes). Local voices note white beans, limas and field peas are equally traditional. Ham hock is the common enrichment.

name: Red Lentil Soup with Lemon
headnote: Melissa Clark's take on mercimek corbasi, the Turkish red lentil soup - light, spicy and distinctly red rather than the usual brown, and done in under an hour. Onion and garlic are sauteed, then tomato paste, cumin and chile powder are cooked in to deepen them before broth, water, red lentils and carrot go in for a 30-minute simmer. Half the pot gets pureed so the texture lands between chunky and smooth, and lemon juice at the end lifts the cumin and chile.
comment_digest: The highest-voted comment (3,440) calls this essentially daal missing its seasonings, and rebuilds it with ginger-garlic paste and fresh chopped tomatoes in place of tomato paste. Just behind it (3,422 votes), a cook uses chicken stock and a 14-ounce can of diced tomatoes instead of the water. The most actionable correction (2,196 votes) is that there is too much liquid for the lentils - either cut the water or add a diced potato or two for body; another popular ratio (1,299 votes) is 1.5 cups lentils to 5 cups chicken broth and no water, with grated carrot sauteed in with the garlic. Note the yield (1,265 votes): it makes four small bowls, so double it to serve four to six. More lemon than called for is near-universal.
flags: NYT has renamed the page 'Red Lentil Soup' (URL redirects to /1016062-red-lentil-soup); same recipe

name: Rice Noodles with Spicy Pork and Herbs
headnote: Tejal Rao writes up a cold rice-noodle bowl with Yunnan roots: noodles dressed in vinegar and chile oil under spicy ground pork, fresh herbs and peanuts, with the garnishes changing by kitchen and season. It goes together quickly but is meant to be eaten slowly, either plated or spread out so people build their own. The chef Simone Tong, whose Manhattan restaurant inspired it, adds raw breakfast radishes and lacto-fermented pickles for crunch, and the headnote invites you to improvise.
comment_digest: Black vinegar is the sticking point, and the top comment (476 votes) gives a workable substitute: one part rice vinegar, one part balsamic, one to three parts water. Others identify the real thing as Chinkiang fermented black rice vinegar, available online or in Chinese groceries; a separate note (104 votes) relays Nina Simonds's suggestion of Worcestershire as a stand-in. The most useful cooking correction (191 votes) is to double the sauce, since the pork seasoned only with garlic, ginger and scallions tastes plain on its own - stir some sauce and herbs into the meat rather than leaving them all as garnish. Enthusiasm runs high (307 votes calling it a top-three recipe), and the herb quantity is meant to be generous, not a sprinkle.

name: Rigatoni with White Bolognese
headnote: Amanda Hesser's version of a meat sauce built without tomato - a variation she notes is seldom encountered in the United States. The headnote is a single line and offers no technique guidance.
comment_digest: The best practical tip (503 votes) is to use your widest-bottomed pot, which cuts the long reduction of wine, broth and mushroom liquid substantially. Another well-voted note (415) says to stagger the soffritto rather than dumping it in together, though commenters argue about the order - a reply (198 votes) points out carrots need far longer than onion, so carrot first makes more sense. Nutmeg is widely considered non-negotiable for a real bolognese (352 votes). The top comment (585 votes) reports a vegetarian version, swapping a pound of sliced mushrooms for the beef and skipping the cream entirely, with good results. One recurring gripe questions cooking in extra-virgin olive oil given its low smoke point.

name: Rishia Zimmern’s Chicken with Shallots
headnote: A one-pot midweek braise that reached The Times in 2014 through Andrew Zimmern's Twitter account, where he posted his then wife Rishia's compressed adaptation of a Martha Stewart recipe: brown thighs and shallots, add wine, tarragon and Dijon, simmer, reduce, finish with cherry tomatoes. Sam Sifton says the kitchen has been tinkering with it since. Serve bread alongside for the sauce.
comment_digest: The single most-endorsed change (1,384 votes) is to finish the dish uncovered in the oven, because the covered simmer leaves the chicken skin soft; a detailed no-splatter variant (603 votes) sautes the shallots in butter in an oven-proof pan, nestles in bone-in thighs and bakes at 400F. A long-standing ambiguity (1,268 votes) is what counts as a shallot: one lobe or both halves of a double shallot, which changes the quantity significantly. Several cooks find the full wine measure too sour and cut it, replacing part with broth (909 votes). Substitutions reported as successful: thyme and bay for tarragon, a splash of cognac with the wine, skinless thighs. Leftovers are said to improve.

name: Riso Al Forno with Crab and Shrimp
headnote: A rice casserole pitched as a relaxed dinner-party main: it takes any shellfish you like, from shrimp to lobster, and forgives timing because it is not served straight from the pot. The rice can be cooked and the shellfish folded in up to two hours ahead, then topped with shrimp and crumbs and baked before serving.
comment_digest: Nearly the whole comment set is one argument: the recipe leaves the shrimp in their shells, and guests do not want to peel shrimp at the table. The three highest-voted notes (69, 50, 40) all object, adding that breadcrumbs scattered over unpeeled shrimp are wasted since the coating comes off with the shell. The constructive version (53 votes) peels the shrimp and simmers the shells into a quick stock to cook the rice in, which puts the shell flavor into the dish instead of on the plate. A cook who peeled ahead and used slightly over a pound reports the shrimp did not dry out (19 votes), so the shells are not needed as protection. A minority defends eating them shell-on with a discard bowl.

name: Roasted Brussels Sprouts with Garlic
headnote: Mark Bittman's roasted brussels sprouts, which NYT calls its most popular version and positions as a default Thanksgiving side. The claim is that this plain treatment caramelizes the sprouts sweet enough to convert skeptics. It comes from a Minimalist column about cast iron.
comment_digest: Burning is the recurring problem: a much-voted account (539) followed the directions and got sprouts burnt to a crisp at 20 minutes, and NYT itself replied in a highly rated note (1,143 votes) that the recipe was revised downward to 10-20 minutes at 400F with a few shakes of the pan. Commenters also mock the instruction to cook 'undisturbed' until the bottoms brown (930 votes) as unverifiable without looking. The most-voted comment (2,763) is a make-ahead question for Thanksgiving, echoed by others (429) - a strong signal people want a reheat plan the recipe does not give. A popular alternative (1,707 votes) is Ina Garten's method: halve, toss in about 1.5 tablespoons of oil, roast at 450F, using far less oil than here. Dried cranberries and walnuts stirred in at the end are a favorite addition.

name: Roasted Cauliflower with Pancetta, Olives and Crisp Parmesan
headnote: Melissa Clark's roasted cauliflower loaded with olives, pancetta and Parmesan that crisps and browns at the edges, offered either as a vegetarian-leaning main or a side to meat, fish or pasta. The recipe assumes finely diced packaged pancetta that dissolves into the sauce; dicing it yourself into half-inch cubes and adding it with the cauliflower gives a chunkier result, and it can be left out entirely to make the dish vegetarian.
comment_digest: The substantive criticism (208 votes) is that the finished dish is too oily, and points at the quarter cup of olive oil in the dressing as the culprit - cut it back. Bacon substitutes for pancetta but should be pre-rendered and added to the partly roasted cauliflower rather than raw (120 votes), otherwise it steams. On olives, a helpful note (152 votes) recommends mild, meaty Castelvetrano over saltier varieties. A well-liked variation (191 votes) adds a can of rinsed chickpeas before roasting - they crisp up - and swaps Aleppo pepper and lime for the flakes and lemon. The top two comments are unanswered questions about a non-meat substitute (anchovies suggested) and a milder seasoning than red pepper flakes, plus confusion over what 'grated' Parmesan means.
flags: top-voted comments are questions rather than tested advice

name: Roasted Potatoes with Sage and Garlic
headnote: The headnote is mostly a short history of sage, whose Latin name salvia means safe or whole, and which served as a medieval cure-all for everything from digestion to headaches. Its argument is that sage suits earthy peasant cooking rather than refined dishes, which is why it works with potatoes and holds up against garlic. Suggested alongside roasted or grilled meat.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (327) says the recipe is more work than it needs to be - the flour dredge does not stick well and adds little. Two better-supported routes to crisp potatoes: cornstarch instead of flour, per Cook's Illustrated (82 votes), or the Irish 'roastie' method (96 votes) of parboiling, draining, shaking the potatoes hard in the pot to rough up the surfaces, then roasting in plenty of hot oil. A cook of 30 years' habit (55 votes) simply drains, shakes, and dumps onto an oiled sheet pan. The parboiling can be done hours ahead (97 votes), which makes it practical for a dinner. Sweet potatoes substitute well. Comment volume is low and the enthusiasm is mostly for the sage-garlic pairing.
flags: NYT has renamed the page 'Garlic Roasted Potatoes With Sage'; same recipe id 298

name: Roasted Salmon Glazed with Brown Sugar and Mustard
headnote: Sam Sifton presents this as a no-recipe recipe you learn once and keep: Dijon and brown sugar mixed to whatever balance of sharp and sweet you like, spread over salted fillets set skin-side down on oiled, foil-lined sheet. Oven at 400F, top half, roughly 12 minutes. Braised greens are the suggested partner.
comment_digest: The top comment (3,190 votes) rewrites the method twice over: skip oiling the foil so the skin sticks and the flesh lifts away cleanly, and broil on the highest rack rather than roast. That second half is disputed by a strongly voted rebuttal (1,138) arguing broiling dries the exposed surface and roasting gives more even, moister fish - so the broil advice is contested, the un-oiled foil trick is not. On the glaze, the most common tweak (2,015 votes) is a teaspoon of ground ginger in the mustard-sugar mix; another popular ratio (1,422 votes) is roughly four parts brown sugar to one part Dijon for a thick paste, sweeter than the recipe implies. A dash of bourbon is a well-liked addition (995 votes).

name: Sautéed Scallops
headnote: Sam Sifton distinguishes the two scallops: sea scallops want a hard sear and a crust, finished with a splash of wine in the butter for acidity against their sweetness, while small bay scallops are better off gently poached in butter. The warning he repeats is against overcooking - he argues an undercooked scallop is essentially not a thing. It comes from a holiday feature.
comment_digest: Dryness is the whole game, and the top three notes (655, 357, 286 votes) all say so. The best refinement: after patting the scallops dry, leave them uncovered in the refrigerator for up to half an hour, which draws out more moisture and gives a noticeably better sear. Equally important is pan space - scallops must not touch each other or they steam instead of browning, so work in batches. Several cooks bring them to room temperature first, and one from the Bay of Fundy prefers a little olive oil with the butter to raise the smoke point. A frequently repeated step the recipe omits: pull off the small tough side muscle before cooking. Wet-packed scallops will not sear; buy dry-packed if you can.

name: Shakshuka with Feta
headnote: Melissa Clark's one-skillet eggs baked in a tomato and red-pepper sauce seasoned with cumin, paprika and cayenne - dinner food here, breakfast food in Israel, eaten with pita or challah. The sauce goes together on the stovetop, the eggs are nestled into it, and the pan finishes in the oven. The dish comes from North Africa and has countless versions; this one departs from tradition by adding crumbled feta, which softens into creamy pockets.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (2,039) says the oven overcooks the eggs - by the time the whites set, the yolks are hard - and recommends dropping to a stovetop simmer with the lid on instead, which also skips heating the oven; a Tuscan cook (1,157 votes) independently confirms the covered-pan stovetop method as standard. The same top note adds chickpeas or lentils to make it a fuller dinner. A detailed comment from an Algerian cook (1,680 votes) offers family variations: small meatballs for substance, and grilling and peeling the peppers before they go in. Spinach stirred in and thicker diced tomatoes instead of watery ones are common (760 votes). One popular comment (859) defends the recipe exactly as written, conceding only a little anchovy paste.

name: Shrimp Scampi with Orzo - NYT
headnote: The argument is that scampi is really about the pan sauce - garlicky butter cut with white wine, lemon, parsley and red-pepper flakes - so instead of pasta or bread this version simmers orzo directly in it, which glosses the sauce with starch and absorbs the garlic. The shrimp marinate in garlic, lemon zest and pepper flakes while the orzo cooks, then steam on top. Suggested with Caesar salad, broccoli or arugula.
comment_digest: Liquid and timing are where people adjust. The top comment (931 votes) cuts to 1.5 cups of liquid, halves the salt, uses only a quarter teaspoon of pepper flakes and starts tasting the orzo at nine minutes; a second high-voted note (796) independently reports two cups left the shrimp swimming. Timing runs both ways - some find 12 minutes too long (410 votes), others needed 14-plus (375) - so taste rather than trust the clock. Toasting the orzo to a deeper brown before liquid goes in is widely endorsed (926, 560 votes), with the caveat to add the garlic later so it does not burn. One well-voted objection (454) is that simply steaming the marinated shrimp on top leaves a raw-garlic taste; lightly sauteing them first fixes it.
